title: Emergency sub plans: build them once with AI, not the night you're sick
time: 15 min per class, once a semester
summary: Giving it your real schedule and routines, and telling it not to invent the rest, is what makes the plan usable by a stranger.
prompt: Act as an experienced instructional designer. Write a one-day emergency substitute plan for my [grade] [subject] class. It must need zero prep from the sub and use only paper, pencils, and what's in a typical classroom. Use my real schedule: [paste times]. Use my real routines: [attendance, bathroom, lining up, quiet signal]. If I didn't give you a routine, write "ASK THE TEACHER NEXT DOOR" instead of making one up. Include: a review activity on [recent topic] with an answer key, a quiet independent task, and a 5-minute filler activity. Before you finish, solve every problem and puzzle yourself and make sure each one has exactly one correct answer.

segments.label: The prompt
segments.text: Act as an experienced instructional designer. Write a one-day emergency substitute plan for my [grade] [subject] class. It must need zero prep from the sub and use only paper, pencils, and what's in a typical classroom. Use my real schedule: [paste times]. Use my real routines: [attendance, bathroom, lining up, quiet signal]. If I didn't give you a routine, write "ASK THE TEACHER NEXT DOOR" instead of making one up. Include: a review activity on [recent topic] with an answer key, a quiet independent task, and a 5-minute filler activity. segments.html: Why it works: Giving it your real schedule and routines, and telling it not to invent the rest, is what makes the plan usable by a stranger. Print it, put it in the sub tub, refresh it each semester.

testHtml:
• What came back: A full-day plan that followed the real schedule, used the real routines, and wrote "ASK THE TEACHER NEXT DOOR" for everything we didn't give it (lunch, PE handoff, dismissal) instead of inventing procedures. All answer keys were correct.
  • What went wrong first: The 5-minute filler was a broken riddle with no answer ("greater than 10, less than 20, and in both the 2s and 5s"). The plan then admitted it had no answer, which would leave a sub stuck in front of the class.
  • What we changed: Added the last sentence ("solve every problem and puzzle yourself"). On retest the filler was a clean missing-number activity with a correct key.
  • Your check: It's long (several pages). Cut what your sub won't need, and do the filler yourself once.

testHtml:
• What came back: Version B (harder) was good every time: "elongated," "devour," "declining," plus one real added fact about echoes.

  • What we changed: Asked for short sentences at "about the same length." Plan on 2 minutes fixing Version A yourself. It's still much faster than writing it.

title: Exit ticket examples with answers, and what a wrong answer means
summary: "What a wrong answer might mean" is the key line. It turns an exit ticket into tomorrow's plan.
prompt: Write 5 exit tickets for this [grade] lesson goal: [goal]. Each one should take under 2 minutes and show me whether the student got the main idea. For each, include the answer, a short worked solution, and what a wrong answer might mean (a guess I should check, not a diagnosis).

segments.label: The prompt
segments.text: Write 5 exit tickets for this [grade] lesson goal: [goal]. Each one should take under 2 minutes and show me whether the student got the main idea. For each, include the answer, a short worked solution, and what a wrong answer might mean (a guess I should check, not a diagnosis).

segments.html: Example from our test (3rd grade area), two of the five tickets:

• Count the squares. A 4-by-3 grid of squares: what is the rectangle's area? Answer: 12 square units. If wrong: "An answer of 10 might mean the student counted only the outside squares. Ask them to point to each square they counted."
  • Check someone's thinking. "A rectangle is 4 units long and 3 units wide. Sam says, 'Its area is 4 + 3 = 7 square units.' Is Sam correct?" Answer: No. The rectangle holds 3 rows of 4 squares, so 3 × 4 = 12 square units.
Why it works: "What a wrong answer might mean" is the key line. It turns an exit ticket into tomorrow's plan.

testHtml:
• What came back: 5 tickets on area that built from counting squares to missing side lengths. The wrong-answer notes were specific and correct. An answer of 10 on a 4-by-3 grid means "counted only the outside squares" (there are exactly 10 outside squares). An answer of 8 for a 5-by-3 rectangle means "added the sides."
  • What it got wrong: Nothing. The grid in ticket 1 was drawn with text symbols, so draw it yourself on the printed copy.

summary: A fixed format and a short rubric keep the AI on track. Requiring an exact quote makes it harder for the AI to praise something that isn't there.

Word bank: winter, hibernate, food, scarce, cold, energy, save, body, temperature, breathing, slows

• Starting: Some animals hibernate in ___. / In winter, ___ can be scarce. / Hibernating helps animals save ___.

title: Free social story generator for a classroom routine
summary: Short stories that describe a situation and what to do are called social narratives.
prompt: Write a short class story to teach my [grade] class the routine for [routine, e.g. "a fire drill"]. Use our real steps: [list the steps]. Write it in first person ("I"), present tense, in short sentences a [age]-year-old can read. Describe what happens, how it might feel (loud, surprising), and what I can do, using calm, positive words. Say what to do, not just what not to do. 8 to 12 sentences. Don't add steps I didn't give you. After the story, list situations my steps don't cover that a student might worry about (for example, being out of the room when the alarm rings), as questions for me.

segments.html: Use it for the whole class, not one child: this card is for routines everyone does (fire drills, a sub day, a new lunch line). Don't ask AI to write a behavior plan for a specific student. Common Sense Media found AI teacher assistants suggested harsher plans for students with Black-coded names than for white-coded names given the same description, and called behavior plans one of the riskiest uses. (Google and MagicSchool said they couldn't reproduce the result.)

segments.label: The prompt
segments.text: Write a short class story to teach my [grade] class the routine for [routine, e.g. "a fire drill"]. Use our real steps: [list the steps]. Write it in first person ("I"), present tense, in short sentences a [age]-year-old can read. Describe what happens, how it might feel (loud, surprising), and what I can do, using calm, positive words. Say what to do, not just what not to do. 8 to 12 sentences. Don't add steps I didn't give you. After the story, list situations my steps don't cover that a student might worry about (for example, being out of the room when the alarm rings), as questions for me.

segments.html: Example from our test (a fire drill):

"The fire alarm rings, and it sounds loud. I might feel surprised, but I know our routine. I stop what I am doing and leave everything. I line up at the door by my table number. I walk silently behind my teacher. I go out the side door to the blacktop. I stand in our line by the fence. I wait silently while my teacher counts everyone. I walk back in when my teacher says it is time."

Why it works: Short stories that describe a situation and what to do are called social narratives. The research behind them is mostly with autistic students, so using one for a whole-class routine is a reasonable stretch, not a tested result. Giving it your real steps keeps it from inventing procedures.

testHtml:
• What came back: A 9-sentence story that used every one of our steps, in order, and added none: "I stop what I am doing and leave everything. I line up at the door by my table number."
  • What went wrong first: The first story was fine, but it skipped the last instruction. We asked it to list anything important that was missing, and it listed nothing, even though our steps never say what to do if you're in the bathroom when the alarm rings.
  • What we changed: Asked it to list situations our steps don't cover, with that one example. On retest it asked 5 good questions, including "What should I do if our usual way out is blocked?" and "What can I do if the alarm feels too loud or I feel scared?"
  • Your check: Answer those questions with your school's real procedures before you read the story to the class.

title: Lab safety check: find the hazards in a lab procedure before students run it
time: 5 min, plus time with the safety data sheets
summary: Quoting the step makes it point at your procedure instead of reciting general lab rules.
prompt: Here is a lab procedure my [grade] [course] students will do: [paste the procedure, including chemicals, concentrations, and amounts]. Act as a careful high school lab safety reviewer. List every real safety problem you find, most dangerous first: missing protective equipment, steps in an unsafe order, chemicals that shouldn't be mixed or heated, missing cleanup or disposal steps, and directions students could misread. Don't pad the list with steps that are fine. Never tell me the procedure is safe: a qualified person at my school decides that. If you find no problems, say "no problems found." For each problem, quote the step, say in plain words what could go wrong, and give a specific fix. Then list what you couldn't check from the text alone (like ventilation, eyewash access, or supervision), and what I should look up in the safety data sheet for each chemical. Don't make up chemical facts: if you aren't sure about a hazard, say so.

segments.html: Read this first: this is a second set of eyes, not a safety review. Your school's chemical hygiene plan, the safety data sheet (SDS) for each chemical, and your department head have the final say. AI can miss a hazard, and it can state a chemical fact wrong with total confidence. It also can't see your room: ventilation, the eyewash, and how many adults are supervising are on you.

For each problem, quote the step, say in plain words what could go wrong, and give a specific fix. Then list what you couldn't check from the text alone (like ventilation, eyewash access, or supervision), and what I should look up in the safety data sheet for each chemical. Don't make up chemical facts: if you aren't sure about a hazard, say so.

segments.html: Why it works: Quoting the step makes it point at your procedure instead of reciting general lab rules. For safety, we ask for every problem, not a top 5, so a sixth hazard can't fall off the list. "Never tell me the procedure is safe" keeps a chatbot from signing off on something only a qualified person should approve, and the SDS list sends you to the real authority.

testHtml:
• What came back: We wrote a magnesium and hydrochloric acid lab with 6 planted hazards, and it caught all 6: an apron but no goggles, water poured into the acid, a stopper pressed into a tube that makes hydrogen, a "deep sniff" of the gas, a Bunsen burner held under the reaction, and "wipe it off with a paper towel" for acid on skin. It opened with "Do not use this procedure as written" and explained the stopper plainly: "Pressure can eject the stopper or break the glass, spraying acid."
  • Does it invent problems? On a safe version of the same lab, it flagged smaller fixes, not made-up dangers. The best one: our "tell the teacher right away and rinse" could make a student go find the teacher before rinsing.
  • What we changed: After review, the prompt no longer lets it call a lab safe, and it now lists what it couldn't check from the text alone. We retested both labs: it still caught all 6 hazards, listed what it couldn't check (ventilation, eyewash and safety-shower access, supervision), and never called either lab safe.
  • Your check: It ranked the missing goggles 6th of 8. You'd rank that higher. Check every chemical fact against the SDS, and have your department head look at any lab you change.

In the strong one, the reasoning must explain why the evidence supports the claim using this science idea: [idea]. Don't just repeat the data. In the weak one, make the mistakes students this age really make (like a claim with no data, or reasoning that just restates the evidence). Label each part [Claim], [Evidence], [Reasoning]. After the weak one, list its mistakes so I can have students find them first. Keep each paragraph under [80] words.

segments.html: Example from our test (6th grade, does water temperature change how fast sugar dissolves?):

Strong: "[Claim] Sugar dissolves faster in warmer water. [Evidence] Dissolving took 95 seconds at 10 degrees C, 61 seconds at 25 degrees C, 34 seconds at 50 degrees C, and 18 seconds at 75 degrees C. [Reasoning] Water particles move faster when water is warmer, so they hit the sugar more often and with more energy. These collisions help separate sugar particles and spread them through the water faster, explaining the shorter dissolving times."

Weak: "[Claim] Sugar dissolves faster in warmer water. [Evidence] The sugar took longer to dissolve in cold water and less time in hot water. [Reasoning] This proves my claim because the warmer the water was, the faster the sugar dissolved."

Why it works: Reasoning is the part students find hardest, the "why does this evidence matter?" step. A weak model next to a strong one, built on the data your class actually collected, gives them something concrete to fix.

testHtml:
• What came back: Two models under our 80-word limit (73 and 39 words) that copied all four times exactly. The strong reasoning used the particle idea instead of repeating the data. The mistake list caught the missing numbers, the reasoning that "repeats the pattern instead of explaining why it happens," and the word "proves."
  • What we changed: After review, we added "if a result doesn't fit the pattern, tell me first, and don't change or leave out any numbers," then tested messy data: our 50-degree trial took 72 seconds, slower than 25 degrees. It flagged that right away ("the pattern is not consistent"), kept the 72, and its strong model said warmer water "generally" works faster and named the result that "does not fit." With the clean data it said "Every result fits the pattern."

title: Number talks for the week: one problem a day, with the strategies kids will use
time: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the steps
summary: A number talk only works if you can hear a strategy and recognize it fast.
prompt: Plan 5 number talks for my [grade] class, one per day, 5 to 10 minutes each. We are working on [skill, e.g. "adding two-digit numbers in your head"]. For each day give me: one problem to show the class, 2 to 4 strategies students this age might use, each written step by step the way a student would say it, one common wrong answer and the thinking behind it, and one question I can ask to push the discussion. Pick numbers that make more than one strategy useful. Write math as plain text, like 38 + 25. Each strategy must work cleanly with that day's numbers, with no false starts. The common wrong answer must come from a real misunderstanding kids this age have (like place value or forgetting to regroup), not a basic fact error like 4 + 5 = 11. Do the mistaken steps yourself to make sure they lead to that wrong answer. Solve every problem and check every step of every strategy yourself.

segments.html: Example from our test (3rd grade, Day 2):

• Add in parts: "47 + 20 = 67. Then 67 + 6 = 73."
  • Make a ten first: "I split 26 into 3 and 23. 47 + 3 = 50. Then 50 + 23 = 73."
  • Combine tens and ones: "40 + 20 = 60. 7 + 6 = 13. Then 60 + 13 = 73."
Common wrong answer: 63. "40 + 20 = 60. 7 + 6 = 13. I put the 3 ones with 60 and got 63." The student drops the extra ten in 13: 60 + 3 = 63.
Discussion question: "Where can we see the new ten in each strategy?"

Why it works: A number talk only works if you can hear a strategy and recognize it fast. Having the likely strategies and the common wrong answer written out ahead of time lets you record kids' thinking on the board instead of puzzling over it.

testHtml:
• What came back: Five number talks for 3rd grade, from 34 + 25 up to 68 + 57, which crosses 100. We worked every step of all 15 strategies, and every one was right. Each day's wrong answer comes from a real place-value slip, like 63 for 47 + 26.
  • What went wrong first: Day 1's "common wrong answer" was 511, which only happens if a child thinks 4 + 5 = 11. One strategy also changed its mind halfway through: "Actually, that didn't make it friendlier."
  • What we changed: Asked for strategies with no false starts and wrong answers from a real misunderstanding, not a fact error, and told it to do the mistaken steps itself. On retest, Day 1's wrong answer became 41: "The student treats the 2 tens as 2 ones."
  • Your check: Show the problem, not the strategies. The strategies are for you, so you can recognize what kids say.

title: Guided notes template from your own slides
summary: Guided notes let students listen instead of copying every word, and the blanks keep them following along.
prompt: Here are my notes for tomorrow's [grade] [subject] lesson: [paste your slides or notes]. Turn them into a one-page guided notes handout. Keep my order and my wording. Replace about [10] key words with blanks: only words that matter (vocabulary, key numbers, causes and effects), never small words like "the" or "is." Each blank must be a word or short phrase that appears in my notes, so students can find it while I teach. If you blank a word, blank it everywhere it appears on the handout except the title, so the page doesn't give away its own answers. Number every blank. Make every blank the same length, like ________, so the length doesn't give the answer away. Add 2 short "In your own words" questions at the end. Then give me an answer key that lists every numbered blank in order with the exact word from my notes. Don't add facts that aren't in my notes.

segments.html: Before you paste: take student names, photos, and any notes about specific students out of your slides first.

Then give me an answer key that lists every numbered blank in order with the exact word from my notes. Don't add facts that aren't in my notes.

segments.html: Example from our test (9th grade biology, photosynthesis):

• Photosynthesis happens in the (1) ________, mostly in leaf cells.
  • (2) ________ contain (3) ________, a green pigment that absorbs light energy.
  • The (6) ________ happen in the (7) ________ and capture light energy.
  • The (8) ________ happens in the (9) ________ and uses that energy to build glucose.
Answer key: 1. chloroplasts, 2. Chloroplasts, 3. chlorophyll, 6. light-dependent reactions, 7. thylakoids, 8. Calvin cycle, 9. stroma.

Why it works: Guided notes let students listen instead of copying every word, and the blanks keep them following along. Building them from your own slides means the blanks match what you actually say.

testHtml:
• What came back: A one-page photosynthesis handout with 10 numbered blanks, all the same length, in our order and our wording, plus an answer key that matched. It added no facts.
  • What went wrong first: The page answered its own blanks. It blanked "chloroplasts" in one line and printed the word again in the very next one: "Chloroplasts contain (3) ________." Carbon dioxide, glucose, and oxygen were also blanked in one place and printed in another.
  • What we changed: First we told it not to blank a word that's printed elsewhere. It obeyed, but it dodged the key terms and blanked filler like "growth" and "underside." So we asked it to blank a word everywhere it appears. On the third try both "chloroplasts" spots were blanks, and the blanks were real vocabulary: chlorophyll, thylakoids, stroma, Calvin cycle.
  • Your check: Read the page once as a student. Could you fill any blank from somewhere else on the page?

title: Spaced review warm-ups from what you've already taught
time: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the key
summary: Coming back to old topics after a gap, and making students pull the answer from memory, are two of the best-supported study moves in learning research.
prompt: Here are the topics my [grade] [subject] class has learned so far this year, with the week we taught each: [list]. Make [number] days of 3-question review warm-ups. Each day, mix topics from different times: one from the last 2 weeks, one from 3 to 6 weeks ago, and one from earlier than that. Don't put the same topic on two days in a row. When a topic comes back, ask about it a different way than before (for example a word problem, finding a mistake, or working backward), so the questions don't all follow the same pattern. Questions should make students recall or use the idea, not just recognize it, so no multiple choice and no true or false. Write math as plain text, like 3/4. Solve every question yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Then give me a separate answer key, and a table showing which topic appears on which day so I can check the spacing.

segments.html: Example from our test (7th grade math, Day 4):

1. A student solves x - 7 = -12 and gets x = -19. Find the correct value of x and explain the mistake.
  2. A jacket costs $54 after a 25% discount. What was its original price?
  3. A submarine starts at an elevation of -18 meters and ends at -31 meters. What signed number represents its change in elevation?
Answers: x = -5 (add 7 to both sides instead of subtracting 7), $72, -13 meters.

Why it works: Coming back to old topics after a gap, and making students pull the answer from memory, are two of the best-supported study moves in learning research. The topic table lets you check the spacing in seconds.

testHtml:
• What came back: Five days of 7th grade warm-ups that followed the spacing rule exactly: one topic from the last 2 weeks, one from 3 to 6 weeks ago, one from earlier, and no topic two days in a row. We worked all 15 questions, and every answer in the key was right.
  • What went wrong first: Nothing was wrong, but it was repetitive. Three of the five days asked the same question with new numbers: "Find the constant of proportionality k in y = kx."
  • What we changed: Asked it to ask about a returning topic a different way each time. On retest the old topics came back as a find-the-mistake question ("A student writes -8 x (-3) = -24"), a working-backward percent problem, and word problems about temperature and a submarine. All 15 answers were still right.
  • Your check: With only 2 topics in each time window, the same topics come back every other day. List more topics and you get more variety.

title: Study guide template that matches your test without giving it away
time: 5 min, plus 5 min to work the problems
summary: Paste the list of what the test covers, not the test itself, and the guide can't leak your questions.
prompt: My [grade] [subject] class has a test on [unit]. Here is what the test covers: [list each skill and the kind of question, e.g. "solve two-step equations (4 short problems)"]. Make a one-page study guide students can use at home. For each skill: one sentence on what to remember, one worked example, and 2 practice problems like the test but not copies. Put all the answers in a separate answer section at the bottom. Write math as plain text, like 2x + 3 = 11. Solve every problem yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Only use the skills I listed: don't add skills that aren't on the test.

segments.html: Example from our test (6th grade ratios, one of four skills):
Remember: Divide each price by its quantity; the lower price per unit is the better buy.
Worked example: Rice costs $6 for 3 pounds or $10 for 4 pounds. Which is the better buy? $6 / 3 = $2 per pound. $10 / 4 = $2.50 per pound. The 3-pound bag is the better buy.
Practice: A 4-pound bag of potatoes costs $6. A 6-pound bag costs $8.40. Which bag has the lower price per pound?

Why it works: Paste the list of what the test covers, not the test itself, and the guide can't leak your questions. Practice that makes students pull up and use the skill does more than rereading notes.

testHtml:
• What came back: A one-page 6th grade ratios study guide covering all four skills on our list and nothing extra. We worked the 4 worked examples and all 8 practice problems, and every answer was right. It even included a small trap that shows up on real tests: "Write the ratio of students wearing boots to students wearing sneakers," with the numbers given in the other order.
  • What it got wrong: Nothing.
  • Your check: One answer is $0.625 per pencil. If your class rounds money to the cent, say so in the prompt.

title: Primary source comparison questions with a quote-proof answer key
time: 5 min, plus 5 min to check the quotes
summary: You choose and paste the documents, so the AI is working from real sources.
prompt: Here are two primary sources my [grade] [subject] class is comparing. Document A: [title, author, date, and the text]. Document B: [title, author, date, and the text]. Treat these two texts as the only sources. Write 6 questions that make students compare them: 2 about what each document says, 2 about how they are alike or different, and 2 about each author's purpose or point of view. Every question must be answerable from the two texts. Then give me an answer key that quotes the exact words from the documents that support each answer, word for word. If a question needs outside knowledge, label it "needs background" and say what students need to know.

segments.label: The prompt
segments.text: Here are two primary sources my [grade] [subject] class is comparing. Document A: [title, author, date, and the text]. Document B: [title, author, date, and the text]. Treat these two texts as the only sources. Write 6 questions that make students compare them: 2 about what each document says, 2 about how they are alike or different, and 2 about each author's purpose or point of view. Every question must be answerable from the two texts. Then give me an answer key that quotes the exact words from the documents that support each answer, word for word. If a question needs outside knowledge, label it "needs background" and say what students need to know.

segments.html: Example from our test (8th grade, Declaration of Independence and Declaration of Sentiments):

• "How does Document B change Document A's statement about who is created equal?" Key: A, "all men are created equal"; B, "all men and women are created equal."
  • "How does Document B use Document A's principle of consent to argue against women's exclusion from voting and making laws?"

Why it works: You choose and paste the documents, so the AI is working from real sources. A 7th grade teacher told Education Week that even when a chatbot was loaded with the documents, it sometimes made up a source. Asking for word-for-word quotes lets you catch that in seconds with Ctrl+F.

testHtml:
• What came back: We gave it excerpts from the Declaration of Independence and the Declaration of Sentiments. It wrote 6 good comparison questions, 2 of each kind we asked for. We checked all 16 quotes in the answer key against our text, and all 16 matched word for word.
  • What it got wrong: Nothing false. It said no question needs background knowledge, but 8th graders may not know that "the elective franchise" means the right to vote.
  • Your check: Word-for-word quotes prove it didn't invent text. They don't prove the reasoning is right, so read the answers to the point-of-view questions yourself.

title: Move the thinking where you can see it: redesign an assignment students could hand to a chatbot
summary: No assignment is AI-proof, but grading the steps along the way, not just the final product, makes the steps worth doing.
prompt: Here is an assignment for my [grade] [subject] class: [paste the directions and due date]. Students could hand most of it to a chatbot. Redesign it so more of the thinking happens where I can see it, without making it longer for students. Keep the learning goal, the final product, and the assignment's requirements the same. I teach [number] students, so keep the added grading under [number] minutes total. Suggest up to 4 changes, like a short in-class step, a checkpoint I grade, a quick conversation, or a choice that uses something only my class did. For each change, say how many minutes of class time it takes and how many minutes of my grading time it adds. Don't claim any change makes cheating impossible. Then rewrite the directions with the changes in, in plain words students can follow. Copy my requirements into the new directions word for word and don't add any. After the directions, list every requirement you changed or added, or write "none."

testHtml:
• What came back: For a 10th grade argument essay: 10 minutes of planning in class with the articles, a quick "ready" or "revisit" mark on each plan, and 15 minutes to start the essay in class. Total: 27 minutes of class time and "about 38 minutes of added grading" for 150 students. It said the steps "won't make cheating impossible."

Its new directions added "Use evidence from both articles," a rule we never set. It also ignored scale: one step added a minute of grading per student, which is 2.5 hours for 150 students.
  • What we changed: Gave it our class size and a grading budget, which it kept on the next try. It still added the "both articles" rule, so we told it to copy our requirements word for word and list anything it changed. On the third try the requirements matched ours exactly.
  • Your check: Put its directions next to yours. The list of changes at the end makes that fast.

title: National History Day banned generative AI. Sort what's allowed for your students.
summary: As of October 1, 2026, National History Day says students "may not use generative AI for research, analysis, design, or creation of their projects," and breaking the rule may mean disqualification.
prompt: Here is National History Day's AI policy: [paste the policy text from NHD's AI guidance]. My [grade] students keep asking whether specific tools are OK for their NHD projects. Sort each of these into "Allowed," "Not allowed," or "Ask NHD," using only the policy I pasted: [list, e.g. "Grammarly rewriting a sentence," "Google Translate on a Spanish-language source"]. For each, quote the line from the policy that decides it. If the policy doesn't clearly decide it, put it in "Ask NHD" and say what's unclear. Then turn the result into a half-page student handout in plain words.

segments.html: What changed: As of October 1, 2026, National History Day says students "may not use generative AI for research, analysis, design, or creation of their projects," and breaking the rule may mean disqualification. The rule covers student projects entered in NHD contests, not how you teach. Still allowed: spelling and grammar checkers, bibliography generators like EasyBib and NoodleTools, and Canva for fonts, borders, and adjusting an existing image's brightness and clarity. Not allowed: Canva's AI tools to create images, generate text, or change historical images. Judge the feature, not the brand: the same app can have an allowed tool and a banned one. Students who used AI before October 1 only to brainstorm topics or keywords, find library resources, or simplify a source's language won't be penalized, but they must cite the tools and explain how they used them in their process paper and annotated bibliography. Use of AI as an accessibility support is decided case by case with contest officials.

Sort each of these into "Allowed," "Not allowed," or "Ask NHD," using only the policy I pasted: [list, e.g. "Grammarly rewriting a sentence," "Google Translate on a Spanish-language source"]. For each, quote the line from the policy that decides it. If the policy doesn't clearly decide it, put it in "Ask NHD" and say what's unclear. Then turn the result into a half-page student handout in plain words.

segments.html: Example from our test (8th grade student handout, excerpt):
Not allowed: "Accept Grammarly's AI rewrite of a whole sentence." "Use Google's AI Overview for project research." "Use Canva's AI photo editor to remove scratches from historical photos."
Ask your teacher to check with NHD: "Google Translate: The policy does not clearly explain whether translating a historical source is allowed."

Why it works: Students don't ask about "generative AI." They ask about Grammarly and Google Translate. Quoting the policy line for each answer lets you check the sort in a minute, and "Ask NHD" keeps it from guessing on the gray areas.

testHtml:
• What came back: We gave it NHD's policy and 12 things 8th graders ask about. Every call matched the policy. Allowed: spell check, NoodleTools, Google search, and brightening a scan in Canva. Not allowed: Grammarly rewriting a sentence, ChatGPT topic ideas, Gemini summarizing a source, Google's AI Overview, and Canva's AI fixing a historical photo. It put Google Translate and text-to-speech for a student with a reading disability in "Ask NHD," which is right: the policy doesn't settle either one.
  • What it got wrong: Nothing. We checked all 12 policy quotes against the text, and every one matched.
  • Your check: Paste the policy from NHD's site, not from memory, and update the handout if NHD changes its guidance.

title: Guided Learning in Google Classroom: write the one source Gemini will teach from
tool: Gemini in Google Classroom, plus any chatbot to draft the source
verdictDetail: worked first try (we tested the prompt that drafts the source in a plain chat, not Guided Learning itself)
summary: Rolling out since November 3, 2026, you can attach a Guided Learning activity to any Google Classroom assignment.
prompt: I'm making a one-page study source for a Guided Learning activity in Google Classroom. Gemini will tutor my [grade] students using this page, so it must be correct and complete. Topic: [skill]. Here is how I teach it: [paste your steps, vocabulary, and one example]. Write the page with: the goal in one sentence, key vocabulary with kid-friendly definitions, the steps in the order I teach them, 2 worked examples with every step shown, the 3 most common mistakes and how to fix each, and 3 practice problems with answers. Use my method and my words, not a different method. Write math as plain text, like 3/4. Solve every problem yourself and make sure each has exactly one correct answer. Then list anything you added that wasn't in what I gave you.

segments.html: What changed: Rolling out since November 3, 2026, you can attach a Guided Learning activity to any Google Classroom assignment. Google says it's designed to give students step-by-step guidance rather than the answer, using the sources you attach. That's a design goal, not a guarantee, so try to get answers out of it yourself in the preview. You can see class and student insight summaries plus student chat transcripts. Your admin has to turn the Gemini app on for you and your students.

The catch: Google's help page says the instructions you type "are for students, and will not be referenced by Gemini." You can attach up to 5 sources, and Google recommends 1. So the source does the steering, and a short, correct one-page source that teaches the way you teach is worth the time.

How to do it: In Classroom, go to Classwork, then Create, then Assignment. Under Attach, pick Guided Learning, name it, add your source, then click Create and preview and try it as a student before you assign it. Make sure students can open the source file. Google says insights are AI-generated, can make mistakes, and are not meant for assessment or placement, so read the transcripts behind them. Transcripts only show if Gemini activity is turned on, and if your admin lets students delete chats, deleted chats disappear from your view.

Privacy: students' chats with the activity become records your teacher view can see, even though you never typed a name. Tell students that before they start, and check your district's rules on Gemini in Classroom before you assign it.
